listing.delivered_by: Mr Arun Rohamally, Senior District Magistrate
listing.title: Mohammad Nowsad Noorbux v Police

text:
Mohammad Nowsad Noorbux v Police
2026 LPW 125
IN THE DISTRICT COURT OF LOWER PLAINES WILHEMS
PCN: 1988/26
In the matter of –
MOHAMMAD NOWSAD NOORBUX
Applicant
v/s
POLICE
Respondent
RULING
1.
The Applicant stands provisionally charged with one Count of drug dealing,
one Count of possession of dangerous drugs and one Count of money laundering. He
has moved to be admitted to bail and was legally represented at the hearing.
2.

The motion was objected to on two grounds, namely –
(a)

risk of absconding; and

(b)

risk of re-offending.

3.
PS Roopnarain, the Enquiring Officer, deponed on behalf of the Respondent to
sustain the grounds of objection. Thereafter, the Applicant made a brief statement
from the dock.
4.
I have taken into account the constitutional right to liberty, as enshrined in
section 5(3) of the Constitution, the Bail Act and the rationale of bail as explained in
the cases of Maloupe (2000 SCJ 223), Hurnam (2004 PRV 53), Labonne (2005
SCJ 38), Deelchand (2005 SCJ 215) and Marthe (2013 SCJ 386).
5.
I have considered all the evidence adduced during the hearing and carried out
the required balancing exercise.
6.
Without going into the merits of the matter, I note that the nature of evidence
against the Applicant appears to be strong inasmuch as he has admitted the seizure.
7.
In relation to the 1st ground of objection, the Enquiring Officer has stated that,
bearing in mind the value of the alleged drugs secured, the Applicant is likely to be
Page 1 of 4

 prosecuted for a serious offence before the Intermediate Court and he may be
amenable to a severe penalty if convicted such that he may abscond if released on
bail out of fear of that potentially severe penalty.
8.
The Enquiring Officer confirmed, under cross-examination, that the Applicant
works as driver. That being the case, it would appear that the Applicant is a person
of limited means. Absconding from a jurisdiction or evading justice from within a
jurisdiction requires some significant resources. Resources which the Applicant
apparently lacks. I have also factored in that there is in force against the Applicant a
Prohibition Order that will continue to remain in force should he be released on bail.
9.
From the document produced, it would appear that the Applicant has, in the
past, been convicted of drug-related offences twice. It would also appear that, at the
time of his arrest, the Applicant was already on bail for a cognate offence of drug
dealing. No evidence was ushered by the Enquiring Officer of any attempt by the
Applicant to abscond or escape from custody in any of those instances and, in the
absence of such evidence, I am led to the ineluctable conclusion that there has been
no such attempt previously.
10.
The Enquiring Officer could not enlighten the Court whether or not the
Applicant has breached bail conditions in the past. This is very telling bearing in
mind the fact that the Applicant has previously been convicted for drug-related
offences and has been provisionally charged with a cognate offence. When these are
considered altogether, it more likely than not that the Applicant will comply with bail
conditions and surrender to the criminal justice system if ever he is admitted to bail.
11.
Additionally, the Enquiring Officer confirmed, under cross-examination, that
the Applicant has a fixed place of abode. This further dwindles the risk of absconding.
12.
It would appear that the 1st ground of objection is premised solely on the
seriousness of the offence with which the Applicant stands provisionally charged.
However, the seriousness of an offence cannot be treated as an all but conclusive
reason for refusing bail – Hurnam (supra).
13.
In the light of the above, I am of the opinion that the 1 st ground of objection is
a mere apprehension of the police and, as such, it fails.
14.
In relation to the 2nd ground of objection, the Enquiring Officer explained that
the Applicant may re-offend, if released on bail, inasmuch as the Applicant has, in
the past, been convicted for drug-related offences and is currently on bail for a cognate
offence and bearing in mind the lucrative nature of the drugs business.
15.
It would appear, from the document produced, that the Applicant has been
convicted –

Page 2 of 4

 (a)

by the District Court of Lower Plaines Wilhems in 2015 for an offence of
simple possession of dangerous drugs; and

(b)

by the District Court of Lower Plaines Wilhems in 2026 for another
offence of simple possession of dangerous drugs.

16.
As highlighted earlier, it would also appear that, at the time of his arrest, the
Applicant was on bail for a similar offence of drug dealing even though the nature of
the dangerous drugs in that case appears to be different from those allegedly secured
in the present matter.
17.
Without prejudice to the principle of presumption of innocence quoad the
Applicant in the matter for which he is currently on bail, the existence of that
provisional charge, when considered together with the criminal record of the
Applicant and the admission made by him in relation to the seizure in the present
matter, gives a clear indication as to a propensity of the Applicant to commit drugrelated offences.
18.
As I have explained earlier, it would appear that the Applicant is a driver by
profession. No other information was provided or solicited during the course of the
hearing on that score and the financial means of the Applicant were also not
canvassed. Being given the nature of the Applicant’s employment, the possibility of
earning easy money through the drugs business might prove a temptation too hard
to resist for the Applicant.
19.
If released, the Applicant would be on bail for two offences of drug dealing for
which the sentence provided is quite significant. As rightly pointed out by the
Enquiring Officer, the Applicant may be driven by the sentiment that he has nothing
to lose in re-offending. This further exacerbates the risk.
20.
Based on the above, I am of the opinion that this 2nd ground of objection has
been well raised.
21.
After anxiously pondering over it, I have reached the conclusion that there is
no condition that I could impose that could reduce the risk substantiated to a
negligible level, the more so as Learned Counsel offered no suggestion as to what
stringent conditions could be imposed on the Applicant (that was not previously
imposed in the other cases for which he has been convicted in the past) that could act
as deterrent this time around.
22.
This is because, even though surety and recognizance requirements might
provide judicial supervision over the Applicant while reporting and curfew
requirements might provide police supervision over him, yet such supervision would
not be on a 24-hour basis thus rendering them nugatory whilst bearing in mind the
circumstances of the present case and the ground of objection substantiated –

Page 3 of 4

 Ravatomanga v The District Magistrate of the Bail and Remand Court & Ors
(2026 SCJ 218).
23.
These conditions (surety, recognizance, reporting and curfew) are the primitive
tools and techniques available as a monitoring mechanism in our present bail
administration model – Islam S. vs Senior District Magistrate, Grand Port
District Court (2006 SCJ 282).
24.
The Applicant may well furnish a substantial surety, he may well appear
periodically in Court pursuant to entering into a recognizance, he may well report to
a police station every day and may well abide by a curfew order, yet, taking into
account the particular circumstances of the present case and the ground of objection
substantiated, the Applicant may as well re-offend once he has left the Court or police
station premises or outside curfew hours.
25.
It is a matter of regret that despite the observations made by the Court in
Islam (supra) as far back as in 2006 and despite amendments having been made to
section 7 of the Bail Act, subsection (4) of that section is yet to be made operative and
an electronic monitoring system is yet to be implemented in Mauritius. Such a system
could have been an effective means of supervision on a 24-hour basis bearing in mind
the circumstances of the present case and the ground of objection substantiated.
26.
Whilst carrying out a balancing exercise, I have taken into account the nature
of the provisional charges lodged against the Applicant, the quite substantial amount
of alleged dangerous drugs involved (the bulk of which appears to be synthetic drugs),
and the devastating and nefarious effect that synthetic drugs are having on our
society. Having done so, I am of the opinion that the greater harm to society far
outweighs the prejudice that may be caused to the Applicant.
27.

The continued detention of the Applicant is, at this stage, still warranted.

28.

I set aside the application.

H. H. A. Rohamally
Senior District Magistrate
14 October 2026
